question:
Patient note:
A 45-year-old man with a background of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, biopsy-proven alcoholic steato-hepatitis diagnosed two years earlier, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease last documented with a baseline creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL was brought to the emergency department by his roommate after being discovered at dawn sprawled across the living-room carpet, drenched in sweat, mumbling incoherently, and clutching his lower abdomen. According to the roommate, the patient had complained for four days of burning dysuria, suprapubic discomfort, and intermittent rigors, had taken no prescribed insulin for 24 hours because of nausea, and had produced scant dark urine despite drinking “jugs of cola.” No oral or parenteral antibiotics, antipyretics, intravenous fluids, or sedatives had been given prior to arrival. During the six-minute ambulance ride he remained un-intubated, coughing weakly yet able to clear secretions, and breathed through a tight non-rebreather mask set at 15 L/min that the crew’s built-in sensor estimated was delivering an inspired fraction of 0.64; oxygen saturations fluctuated in the mid-80s en route, and no positive-pressure device was applied. A single 20-gauge antecubital cannula was placed for a keep-open rate of lactated Ringer’s at 30 mL/h, but no bolus or vasopressor infusion was started. On stretcher entry to the resuscitation bay—before any hospital-initiated therapy—he lay semi-recumbent, diaphoretic, and tachypnoeic with shallow respirations at 32/min, accessory-muscle use of the sternocleidomastoids, and audible end-expiratory groans. Oscillometric vitals recorded immediately showed a heart rate of 132 beats/min in sinus rhythm, an initial blood-pressure reading of 81/43 mm Hg repeated manually with the same result, temperature 38.9 °C tympanic, and pulse oximetry 87 % on the unchanged facemask. Capillary refill exceeded five seconds, the fingertips were cool and mottled, and jugular venous pulsation was not visible at 45°. Pupils measured 3 mm symmetrically and were sluggishly reactive; he opened his eyes only to loud verbal stimuli, uttered inappropriate words that failed to form sentences, and withdrew purposefully from painful nail-bed pressure, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 10. A right radial arterial catheter was seated on the first attempt within three minutes of arrival; the simultaneous blood gas—drawn while he continued to breathe spontaneously on 0.64 FiO₂—demonstrated a pH of 7.25, PaCO₂ 33 mm Hg, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, lactate 5.6 mmol/L, and a PaO₂ of 121 mm Hg. Chest examination revealed coarse crackles at both bases without wheeze; percussion was dull posteriorly, and transmitted voice sounds were mildly increased. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a rapid regular rhythm with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was distended and tender suprapubically with a palpable, firm bladder edge suggesting retention; flank percussion elicited bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness. Skin survey showed spider angiomata over the upper chest, scattered ecchymoses on the shins, and no peripheral edema. A 16-French Foley catheter passed during the primary survey produced 30 mL of cloudy, malodorous urine immediately; the roommate presented a smartphone note used for blood-glucose tracking that documented only 770 mL total voided in the preceding twenty-four hours. Point-of-care ultrasound performed before any crystalloid bolus visualized a thick-walled, dilated bladder with echogenic debris, moderate bilateral hydronephrosis, an underfilled inferior vena cava measuring 0.8 cm collapsing completely with inspiration, and a hyperdynamic left ventricle. Peripheral blood obtained concurrently with the arterial sample—prior to any antibiotics, insulin, fluids, or vasoactive agents—revealed a white-blood-cell count of 24.7 × 10³/µL with 19 % band forms, hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, and a platelet count of 168 000 /µL. Basic metabolic panel showed sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, chloride 96 mmol/L, an anion gap of 22, glucose 468 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 68 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 2.55 mg/dL. Hepatic chemistries returned aspartate aminotransferase 98 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 84 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 246 U/L, international normalized ratio 1.4, and total bilirubin 2.15 mg/dL, predominantly conjugated. High-sensitivity troponin was <0.02 ng/mL, C-reactive protein exceeded 300 mg/L, and serum ketones were positive at 3.8 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph taken while the facemask remained in place demonstrated faint bilateral patchy opacities without focal consolidation, an elevated right hemidiaphragm, and no pleural effusion or pneumothorax. Plain abdominal film showed a distended bladder pushing bowel loops aside but no free air. Twelve-lead electrocardiography recorded sinus tachycardia at 128 beats/min with diffuse peaked T waves and a corrected QT interval of 444 ms. Up to this exact juncture—before a single milliliter of resuscitation fluid, vasopressor, antimicrobial, or insulin had been administered—the patient remained spontaneously breathing through a high-flow facemask delivering 64 % oxygen with an arterial oxygen tension of 121 mm Hg, exhibited a persistently low arterial pressure of 81/43 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, displayed near-normal platelet numbers, had moderate hyperbilirubinemia on a background of chronic liver injury, demonstrated acute kidney insult superimposed on chronic disease with creatinine 2.55 mg/dL and oliguria of 770 mL/day, and showed a depressed sensorium quantified as a Glasgow Coma Score of 10 in the setting of presumed septic bladder outlet obstruction complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis and early acute lung involvement.

Question: What is the patient's Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) Score?
solution:
The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) sums six organ-system scores, each graded 0–4. Use the admission values before resuscitation.
1. Respiratory: PaO₂/FiO₂ = 121/0.64 ≈ 189 mm Hg. This is <300 (2 points). Although it is also <200, he is breathing spontaneously on a mask without positive-pressure support, so the 3-point criterion is not met.
2. Coagulation: Platelets 168,000/µL are ≥150,000/µL (0).
3. Liver: Bilirubin 2.15 mg/dL is in the 2.0–5.9 mg/dL range (2).
4. Cardiovascular: Mean arterial pressure ≈ (81 + 2 × 43)/3 = 55.7 mm Hg, below 70 without vasopressors (1).
5. Neurologic: GCS 10 is in the 10–12 range (2).
6. Renal: Creatinine 2.55 mg/dL is in the 2.0–3.4 mg/dL range (2). Urine output of 770 mL/day is not below 500 mL/day and does not raise the renal score.
Total = 2 + 0 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 9.
Final answer: 9
